overview.headline: Teen saving guide for emergency funds and early compound interest

keyPoints.point: Save at least 10 percent of earnings directly into a savings account for emergencies
keyPoints.quote: Once your teen has a steady job, help them set up a savings program so that at least 10 percent of earnings goes directly into their savings account.

keyPoints.point: Build an emergency fund covering at least three months of living expenses for emergencies
keyPoints.quote: have at least three months’ worth of living expenses saved up in case of an emergency.

keyPoints.point: Compound interest earns interest on both saved money and previously earned interest over time
keyPoints.quote: Compound interest is when your child earns interest on both the money they save and the interest they earn.

keyPoints.point: Starting to save $100 every year at age 14 can grow to about $23,000 by age 65 at 5 percent, versus about $7,000 when starting at age 35
keyPoints.quote: If they set aside $100 every year starting at age 14, they'd have about $23,000 at age 65.

keyTerms.gloss: account at a bank or credit union for holding savings to cover emergency expenses
keyTerms.quote: Once your teen has a steady job, help them set up a savings program so that at least 10 percent of earnings goes directly into their savings account.

keyTerms.gloss: interest earned on both original money saved and accumulated interest
keyTerms.quote: Compound interest is when your child earns interest on both the money they save and the interest they earn.

keyTerms.gloss: percent charged or earned for borrowing or saving, relevant when choosing a bank account
keyTerms.quote: the interest rate may not be as relevant since the goal is to save enough money to cover emergency expenses.

keyTerms.gloss: employer added money that matches employee savings in a 401(k) as an incentive to save
keyTerms.quote: Some employers provide matching contributions as an incentive to save, so it’s smart to save at least enough for the maximum matching contribution.
